overview: Old Calabar was a cluster of Efik trading towns and powerful households on the Cross River waterways, including Duke Town, Creek Town and Old Town. Its history predates this map’s 1878 to 1914 interval, which spans growing British colonial control.

periods.title: A merchant’s earlier diary
periods.summary: Antera Duke recorded business and family life before the mapped period.

periods.title: Treaty and colonial administration
periods.summary: British protection developed into colonial rule; 1914 is a map cutoff, not a securely established date when the chiefs’ authority disappeared.

items.text: A trading “house” meant more than one building. Extended families occupied compounds with buildings around yards; free relatives, wives and enslaved people lived within this unequal social order. Wattle-and-daub construction made the town a landscape of linked homes and family institutions.

Merchants learned trade English through contact and correspondence with visiting sailors. This practical literacy included numbers, measurements and names for imported goods. Antera Duke’s first language was Efik; his written English was a tool he adapted to his own purposes.

His diary opens “I be angiry with my Dear awaw ofion”: “I was angry with my dear [wife] Awaw Ofiong.” The 1785 to 1788 diary survives in transcription. This original trade-English sample reveals personal feelings as well as commerce.

Anchoring a ship involved negotiations and fees called comey. In July 1785, Antera accompanied Duke Ephraim aboard a Liverpool slave ship to collect them. Such payments connected town leaders, merchants and ships; the port’s political institutions were intertwined with the destructive Atlantic slave trade.

Food provisioning was a large business too. The Hannover’s 1720 records list 11,400 yams purchased at Old Calabar, alongside enslaved people. Farmers, carriers and traders supplied the food that kept voyages going. The account exposes both the scale of agricultural work and its connection to forced transport.

A 1914 missionary account describes Hope Waddell Training Institution, founded in 1895, teaching carpentry, printing, bookbinding, engineering and tailoring. A school day could involve making a useful object or preparing printed pages, not only reading them. These were organized vocational courses within a mission institution.

That account also records a change in girls’ education: an initially combined institution separated the girls’ section, with girls’ institutions established elsewhere nearby. This shows how training opportunities were organized by gender. The source describes the mission’s arrangements, not the schooling of every Calabar child.

A covered gourd bowl collected at Calabar by 1911 has its lid secured with twisted fibre cord and its surface decorated by burning designs into it. The museum cautiously attributes it to Ibibio makers. Practical containers could also be carefully decorated objects; a tied lid was a sensible piece of design.

The colonial report for 1906 counted 798 cases at St Margaret’s hospital in Calabar and 7,129 outpatients. Two Catholic sisters assisted with female patients. The report separately described a European hospital, making racial divisions in colonial healthcare visible alongside the work of nurses and patients seeking treatment.

sections.title: Colonial change and a continuing city

items.text: The treaty of 10 September 1884 promised British protection and restricted the chiefs’ dealings with foreign powers. It did not draw a detailed territorial boundary. Its later interpretation became contentious, a reminder that the language of a treaty and the expansion of colonial power were different parts of the story.

The International Court of Justice’s 2002 judgment described British indirect administration and recorded Nigeria’s answer that it could not give a precise date when the chiefs ceased to exist as a distinct entity. A map label ending in 1914 therefore should not be read as a documented, one-day destruction of Old Calabar.

Calabar continued as a city long after these political changes. Its university became a separate institution in 1975 and began teaching in three faculties in October 1976. This later educational history belongs to the living city in Nigeria, rather than extending the old trading polity’s sovereignty into the present.

ending.text: The towns’ autonomy was progressively absorbed into British colonial administration after the 1884 treaty. No exact single ending is established here; Calabar’s people, households and city continued beyond the imported 1914 cutoff.
